title: DFA and NFA
subtitle: The simplest computer: a finite number of states and no memory beyond “where am I?”.

sections.title: Deterministic finite automata
sections.body: A DFA is five things: states Q, alphabet Σ, a transition function δ: Q × Σ → Q, a start state and a set of accepting states. Read the input left to right; each symbol moves exactly one arrow; accept if you end in an accepting state. The machine below accepts binary strings that end in 01: input 1101 → yes, 0101 → yes.

questions.prompt: Why is a DFA called deterministic?

choices.text: From each state, each symbol leads to exactly one next state.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — strings ending in 01
figures.note: Double circle = accepting. The highlighted arrow is the one just taken.

sections.title: Designing a DFA
sections.body: Decide what the states must remember, name one state per distinct situation, then add a transition for every state–symbol pair. For “ends in 01” the machine needs to remember only: nothing useful yet (q0), last symbol was 0 (q1), last two were 01 (q2). For “even number of 1s” two states suffice: even, odd.

questions.prompt: Minimum number of states for “strings with an even number of 1s”?

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: One state cannot tell even from odd.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Even and odd are all it needs to remember.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — an even number of 1s
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"even","engine":"dfa","spec":"start: even
accept: even
even,0 -> even
even,1 -> odd
odd,0 -> odd
odd,1 -> even","input":"1011","width":600,"height":440});

problems.prompt: Design a DFA over {0,1} accepting strings that end in 01. Does it accept 0101?
problems.answer: Use the three-state machine in Figure 2.1.1. 0101 ends in 01, so it is accepted.

sections.title: Nondeterministic finite automata
sections.body: An NFA may have several transitions on the same symbol (or none). It accepts if some sequence of choices reaches an accepting state — equivalently it is in a set of states at once. NFAs are often far easier to write: “the second-to-last symbol is 1” needs 3 NFA states but 4 DFA states. Remarkably NFAs recognise exactly the same languages as DFAs.

questions.prompt: Are NFAs more powerful than DFAs?

choices.text: No — every NFA has an equivalent DFA, though possibly exponentially larger.
No, because NFAs cannot be simulated.

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: They recognise exactly the regular languages.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: They can, by tracking the set of states.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3.1 — second-to-last symbol is 1
figures.note: Several states can be active at once.

sections.title: NFA to DFA: the subset construction
sections.body: Make each DFA state a set of NFA states. Start with {start}; for each set and symbol, the next set is the union of all NFA moves. A set is accepting if it contains an accepting NFA state. An NFA with n states gives at most 2ⁿ DFA states.

worked.why: NFA: q0 loops on 0,1; on 1 also goes to q1; q1 goes to q2 on 0 or 1; q2 accepts.
From {q0} on 1: {q0, q1}. On 0 from {q0, q1}: {q0, q2}. So DFA states include {q0}, {q0,q1}, {q0,q2}, {q0,q1,q2}.

questions.prompt: An NFA with 5 states needs at most how many DFA states?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Every subset of states can occur.

sections.title: ε-transitions
sections.body: An ε-NFA may change state without reading any symbol. Before and after each input symbol, follow all ε-arrows (the ε-closure). Below, from q0 the ε-arrow to q1 means the machine may already “be in” q1, so it accepts aab (a a then b via q1 → q2) but not aa.

questions.prompt: The ε-closure of a state is…

choices.text: The set of states reachable using only ε-moves (including itself).

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Used before and after each symbol.

figures.caption: Figure 2.5.1 — aab is accepted
figures.note: The active set includes the ε-closure.
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"eps1","engine":"nfa","spec":"start: q0
accept: q2
q0,a -> q0
q0,e -> q1
q1,b -> q2","input":"aab","width":600,"height":440});

figures.caption: Figure 2.5.2 — aa is rejected
figures.script:
var lab = create("steplab", {"name":"eps2","engine":"nfa","spec":"start: q0
accept: q2
q0,a -> q0
q0,e -> q1
q1,b -> q2","input":"aa","width":600,"height":440});

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• DFA: one move per symbol. NFA: a set of possible moves. Same power.
  • Design by asking what must be remembered.
  • Subset construction: up to 2ⁿ states.
